beats.narration_text: The definition: vibecoding is when you build a website or app by describing what you want in plain English and letting Claude write all the actual code. You don't write a single line. You vibe your way to a thing that runs. Claude Code is the specific tool for this — it lives in the Code tab of the Claude desktop app. The word 'vibe' is accurate in both the good and the bad sense. You get a running thing faster than you'd expect. The edges are rough. And that's fine, depending on what you're building it for.

There are exactly two good reasons to vibecode. One: you build a clickable version of your idea so that developers and designers stop guessing what you meant. A rough prototype beats a twelve-page requirements document. Send a working website to the dev team and they understand your vision in two minutes. Two: you build a small tool that does one specific thing better than a generic Claude chat interface — just for you, your team, or a handful of customers. If nobody outside that small group sees the rough edges, the rough edges don't matter.

Seven steps to set up Claude Code. One: get the app at claude.com/download, install it, open the Code tab. Two: create a clean folder on your computer, just for this project — nothing private, nothing you'd hate to lose, because Claude will read everything inside it. Three: turn on bypass permissions — without it, Claude asks your approval for every file operation, which slows everything down. Four: point Claude to your folder. Five: describe what you want. Six: review what it builds. Seven: iterate by talking to it, not by editing code manually.

beats.narration_text: The first use case is a mockup for a consulting team to hand to developers. A non-coder can replace an ambiguous verbal description with a rough working website link. The developers see the layout, the flow, the feel. The designer gets the vision. This is not rocket science — it's a communication tool. The value is not in the software quality; it's in eliminating misunderstanding before expensive development starts.

beats.narration_text: The second use case is a custom LinkedIn analytics dashboard. Connect public post data through Apify, calculate an engagement score with your own weighting of likes, comments, and reposts, link every result to the original post, and add topic search. The value is specificity: Claude Code can build the small internal tool that no generic product provides. That's the ceiling of vibecoding: a small, personal, useful thing that nobody else makes exactly this way.

Now the honest limits. Vibecoding fails when the tool needs to be reliable for users who aren't you. Claude Code builds working things; it doesn't build tested, hardened, secure things. It will make mistakes in logic, skip edge cases, and produce code you can't read or debug if something breaks. It's not a substitute for a developer. It's a substitute for a static mockup or a very specific internal spreadsheet. The moment you're building something a customer will pay for, you need a real engineer involved — even if Claude wrote the first draft.

A strong starting prompt pattern for Claude Code. Not 'build me a thing.' Too vague. The pattern that works: describe the one specific job the tool needs to do, who uses it, what inputs it takes, and what output it should produce. Then let Claude ask clarifying questions before it writes any code — because the questions Claude asks will tell you what you hadn't thought through yet. The first session is always more planning than building. That's correct. Changing the plan in plain English costs nothing. Changing the code later costs time.

props.code:
Build me a [type of tool] that does [one specific job]. Who uses it: [me / my team of N / internal only]
Inputs: [what data or files it takes in]
Outputs: [what it produces or shows] Before writing any code, list your top 5 assumptions
and ask me any clarifying questions.
Then build it step by step.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take the specific thing you'd build first — a mockup, a small dashboard, a one-purpose tool — and paste this into Claude Code to start.
